title: Portable and Wireless Charging Solutions
desc: Understand power banks, wireless pads and shared charging kiosks: safety, standards, battery care and a simple service business.
outcomes: Explain how batteries, chargers and wireless pads work.
task: Test and compare three portable chargers, write a safety and quality note, and plan a small shared charging point with price and care rules.
condition: Three chargers (practice or real), a meter or phone app, a spreadsheet, two peers and a mentor. No opening of battery packs.
standard: Capacity test is repeated and averaged; safety rules are followed; unsafe items are rejected; business plan shows costs; peers rate Meets or better.
who: Shop owners, repair techs, event hosts, students.
evidence: test table, safety note, price sheet, plan
modules: Batteries, units and real capacity
Understand
You cannot compare power banks without understanding the units, and the number on the label is not what you can use.
Energy is measured in watt-hours: Wh = volts x amp-hours. A 10,000 mAh cell at 3.7 V holds 37 Wh.
Converting the voltage to 5 V and charging a phone wastes 20 to 40 per cent as heat.
Cycles of charge and discharge age batteries; heat ages them faster.
Labels often quote capacity at cell voltage, not usable output.
A 37 Wh bank at 70 per cent efficiency delivers about 26 Wh, enough for roughly two charges of a 12 Wh phone, not three.
Calculate usable energy for three banks from their labels and assumed efficiency.
Calculate the maths correctly, and state the assumptions.
Wired charging, cables and standards
Understand
Cables and plugs decide speed and safety.
Connector types and power delivery levels set the maximum watts.
Thin or damaged cables overheat and limit current.
Match charger, cable and device; use certified products.
Fast charging needs both ends to agree on voltage.
A 65 W charger with a cheap cable charges a laptop slowly because the cable cannot carry the current; a certified cable restores full speed.
Build a compatibility table for five devices, chargers and cables.
Check that the entries are correct and sourced.
Wireless charging
Understand
Coils and magnetic fields transfer energy without a plug.
Pad and device must align; metal objects between them can heat up.
Efficiency is lower than wired charging, so more heat and wasted energy.
Standards exist for compatibility.
Good for convenience, not always for speed.
A wireless pad at 70 per cent efficiency wastes 30 per cent as heat, so a 15 Wh phone charge draws about 21 Wh from the wall.
Explain how wireless charging works and calculate wall energy for one charge.
Explain the idea and one limit so that a peer can repeat them.
Testing real capacity
Apply
Measure, do not trust the label.
Fully discharge into a known load while recording watt-hours with a meter.
Repeat three times and average.
Compare with the label and record the percentage.
Record temperature and time.
A 20,000 mAh bank labelled 74 Wh delivers 55 Wh on average, 74 per cent of the claim. Its price per delivered Wh is higher than a competitor with an honest label.
Test three banks and record results in a table with price per delivered Wh.
Report results that include averages, percentage of label and cost per Wh.
Safety, quality and transport
Evaluate
Poor batteries can overheat or catch fire.
Look for certification marks and protection circuits.
Avoid swollen, hot or damaged units; isolate them in a safe container.
Follow airline and transport rules for carrying batteries.
Dispose of faulty batteries at a collection point.
A swollen bank is isolated in a metal tin away from flammable items and taken to a collection point the same day.
Write a safety note, inspection routine and disposal procedure.
Include inspection, isolation, transport rule and disposal.
A shared charging service
Create
Kiosks and lending services serve events, cafes and transport hubs.
Locations: cafes, events, transport hubs and gyms.
Pricing by time or deposit; refund on return.
Return, cleaning, serial tracking and loss control.
Staff training, insurance and a complaint route.
A cafe rents banks for 50 INR with a refundable deposit of 300 INR (estimates; check your market) and tracks serial numbers. Loss falls to zero after deposits are introduced.
Plan a small service with prices, loss assumptions and break-even.
Show costs and prices with currency, and calculate break-even.
Care, reuse and recycling
Apply
Extend the life of your devices.
Avoid heat; store at about half charge.
Recycle at collection points; never put batteries in general waste.
Repair only with trained people.
Label and track batteries.
A cafe has a labelled battery recycling box and a monthly collection. Banks are retired after 500 cycles or when capacity falls below 70 per cent.
Write care rules and a retirement rule.
Write specific and measurable rules.
Pilot and review
Create
Test the idea for a week.
Run a trial with a small number of users.
Record use, complaints and losses.
Improve based on data.
Decide whether to continue.
Week one: 40 rentals and 2 losses; a deposit is added and losses stop. Average rental time is 4 hours, so one bank earns about 12 INR an hour.
Present your pilot review.
Use real numbers, and date one improvement.
quiz: What do you do with a swollen bank?
Discharge into a known load and measure Wh.
rubric: Capacity, time and temperature logged for each charger
Logged results repeated once and the spread reported
Fire, heat and shipping rules for lithium batteries are written down
Rules checked on an official page and a storage plan tested
